title: Curiosity Versus Continual Learning
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece separates two qualities that are often conflated in discussions of leadership growth: curiosity and continuous learning. Curiosity is defined as a drive to understand how things work and why people behave as they do, while continuous learning is defined as a drive toward self-improvement and skill acquisition through practice. The author argues these are genuinely distinct capacities — a leader can have one without the other — and that each fuels different outcomes, with curiosity feeding relationships and creative insight while continuous learning builds the skills tied to high achievement. The piece closes by framing the combination of both traits as a rare 'leadership superpower' worth deliberately cultivating in oneself and others.
points: The essay's central distinction is that curiosity and continuous learning are separate capacities with different downstream benefits, not two names for the same trait.
It links curiosity specifically to relationship-building and creative insight, and continuous learning specifically to the skills underlying high achievement.
It frames talent assessment as incomplete unless it screens for both qualities, since most people lean toward only one.
The closing Wooden quote ('what you learn after you know it all') reinforces the continuous-learning half of the argument as an ongoing practice, not a fixed trait.
quotes: Curious leaders investigate and explore. They have a deep desire to understand what makes people tick and tock, how they came to be who they are today, and what drives them toward achievement.
Leaders who focus on self-improvement through continuous learning take a different approach. They jump at any opportunity to learn how to get better.

It seems that relationships and the creative insights that provide the foundation for higher performance benefit most from curiosity, while a fixation on self-improvement through learning and practice most enhances the skills essential for high achievement.
The combination of both qualities is a leadership superpower. The best leaders do their best to develop both attributes in themselves and in others.
Which reminds us of a favorite saying from legendary coach John Wooden, “It’s what you learn after you know it all that counts.
